title: The Loop, Measured: Three Ways to Wait, and What Each Costs in Latency and CPU

questions.question: What is the latency of a reading, in this lesson?
options: The loop's period
The time from when the reading was MADE to when the consumer had it, measured with a stamp carried in the reading
The time the consumer spends working on it
The time between two consecutive readings being looked at
questions.explanation: A loop-time measurement would read 5000 microseconds for every design at 200 Hz. Stamping at the source is the only way to know how long a reading waited.

questions.question: At 200 Hz for 2 seconds, a spinning consumer, a polling one (1 ms) and a sleeping one. Which has the lowest median latency, and what did it cost?
options: The sleeper, at no cost
The spinner, at 0.4 microseconds, which used 1999 ms of CPU in 2000: a whole core
The poller, since 1 ms is short
They were all equal
questions.explanation: The poller's median was 514 to 549 us and its CPU 31 to 32 ms; the sleeper's was 39 to 65 us and 4.7 to 8.9 ms. Nothing is free, and the right choice comes from the budget.

questions.question: A 5 ms producer, a consumer taking 20 ms a reading, and a queue of 4. produced 60, delivered 19. What is dropped, and why must it be reported?
options: Nothing; some readings are just late
41 of 60: a latency figure over the 19 that got through says nothing about the rest, so every reading must be delivered or dropped and the counts must add up
19 readings
The queue's capacity
questions.explanation: The 19 survivors looked healthy, since the queue never held more than four. Conservation, produced equals delivered plus dropped, is the first thing the suite checks.

questions.question: A slow consumer and a full queue. What should the producer do, and how is it checked?
options: Wait until there is room
Drop the reading, count it, and keep its rate: measured, produced plus missed slots stayed at about 60 so the slow consumer did not slow the producer
Stop
Double the queue
questions.explanation: A producer that blocks on a full queue has moved the loss from the queue to the sensor. The slots law checks that the producer's grid was kept.

questions.question: A test asserted that a spinning consumer went round more than 100 times per reading, and failed in 3 of 10 runs with 12 busy loops competing. Why, and what replaced it?
options: The spinner has a bug

With every core busy the spinning thread is descheduled too and goes round far less, so the count depends on the CPU the scheduler grants; it is now printed, and only bounds a slower machine cannot break are asserted: a poller goes round at most about once a millisecond, a sleeper at most once per reading plus its timeouts
The assertion was too strict by a few percent
Spinning does not work under load
questions.explanation: Never gate on a count that scheduling affects. After the change: 0 failures in 12 quiet runs and 0 in 20 loaded runs.

questions.question: Why report the 99th percentile and the worst, and count overflows, instead of a mean?
options: Means are hard to compute
A timing distribution has a hard floor and a long tail, so a mean says almost nothing about the tail, which is the whole question: the sleeper's worst was 473 to 1548 us against a p99 of 167 to 245
Percentiles are faster
Because the histogram cannot compute a mean
questions.explanation: Lesson 07-03's argument, with numbers: one reading in the sleeper's run took 1.5 ms, which was the scheduler and not the queue. A specification written as an average is not a specification.
